x.ASV: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. Jehovah, how are mine adversaries increased! Many are they that rise up against me.
x.Darby: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. Jehovah, how many are they that trouble me, many they that rise up against me!
x.KJV: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me.
x.YLT: A Psalm of David, in his fleeing from the face of Absalom his son. Jehovah, how have my distresses multiplied! Many are rising up against me.

nt: The word **how** marks this as an emotional outburst that is emphasizing to Yahweh how very desperate the author’s situation is. Use an exclamation that would communicate that meaning in your language. Alternate translation: [Oh Yahweh, I have so many enemies]

Here, **risers against me** is an common expression that means “people who rebel against me” or “people who wish to fight me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use an expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Those getting in my face] or [Those who rebel against me]

x.ASV: Many there are that say of my soul, There is no help for him in God. [Selah
x.Darby: Many say of my soul, There is no salvation for him inGod. Selah.
x.KJV: Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God. Selah.
x.YLT: Many are saying of my soul, `There is no salvation for him in God.' Selah.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Surely God will not save him]

This is the first instance of the Hebrew word **Selah**, the meaning of which is unknown. The ancient Greek translation uses a term that means “musical interlude.” Your translation team should decide if you will (1) spell this word to reflect its Hebrew form, “Selah,” or (2) omit “Selah” or (3) translate with a word meaning something like “musical interlude” or “pause” in your language.

x.ASV: But thou, O Jehovah, art a shield about me; My glory, and the lifter up of my head.
x.Darby: But thou, Jehovah, art a shield about me; my glory, and the lifter up of my head.
x.KJV: But thou, O Lord, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
x.YLT: And Thou, O Jehovah, art a shield for me, My honour, and lifter up of my head.

nt: Here, **shield** represents protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are my protection]

Because Yahweh is the actor in all the other actions in this verse, calling **Yahweh** his **glory** probably means that Yahweh gives the psalmist glory or honor. Since the psalmist has just spoken about his enemies and about Yahweh being his protector, he probably means that Yahweh gives him glory by giving him victory over his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who gives me glory] or [the one who gives me victory]

Lifting the author’s **head** could mean (1) giving him courage or (2) giving him victory over his enemies or (3) restoring him to being king of Israel (given the context of David fleeing from his son’s usurping). If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the one who encourages me] or [and the one who lifts me over my enemies] or [and the one who lifts me to the throne]

x.KJV: I cried unto the Lord with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill. Selah.
x.YLT: My voice is unto Jehovah: I call: And He answereth me from his holy hill, Selah.

nt: The implication is that the psalmist is calling to Yahweh for help and that Yahweh’s answer takes the form of giving help. You can include this information if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I call for help … and he helped me]

x.ASV: I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for Jehovah sustaineth me.
x.Darby: I laid me down and slept; I awaked, for Jehovah sustaineth me.
x.KJV: I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me.
x.YLT: I--I have lain down, and I sleep, I have waked, for Jehovah sustaineth me.

nt: אֲנִ֥י שָׁכַ֗בְתִּי וָֽ⁠אִ֫ישָׁ֥נָ⁠ה הֱקִיצ֑וֹתִי כִּ֖י יְהוָ֣ה יִסְמְכֵֽ⁠נִי

The phrase **laid myself down and slept** is not a one-time occurrence but a universal statement about his daily peace because of Yahweh. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases since the second phrase, **for Yahweh protects me**, gives the reason for the result, **I awoke** as well as the reason for the author’s confidence that he can lie down and sleep. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh protects me, I lie down, sleep, and awake]

x.Darby: I will not fear for myriads of the people that have set themselves against me round about.
x.KJV: I will not be afraid of ten thousands of people, that have set themselves against me round about.
x.YLT: I am not afraid of myriads of people, That round about they have set against me.

nt: The psalmist does **not fear** because of Yahweh’s protection, mentioned in verse 5. Be sure that connection is clear in your language.

x.ASV: Arise, O Jehovah; save me, O my God: For thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; Thou hast broken the teeth of the wicked.
x.Darby: Arise, Jehovah; save me, myGod! For thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheekbone, thou hast broken the teeth of the wicked.
x.KJV: Arise, O Lord; save me, O my God: for thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly.
x.YLT: Rise, O Jehovah! save me, my God. Because Thou hast smitten All mine enemies on the cheek. The teeth of the wicked Thou hast broken.

nt: The psalmist is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to ask Yahweh to take action. He is not telling him to get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action] or [Do something]

The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [oh God whom I worship]
הִכִּ֣יתָ אֶת־כָּל־אֹיְבַ֣⁠י לֶ֑חִי שִׁנֵּ֖י רְשָׁעִ֣ים שִׁבַּֽרְתָּ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms (../front/intro.md) for more information. The phrases **my enemies** and **the wicked** refer to the same group of people. Alternate translation: [you hit all my enemies on the jaw; you even break those wicked enemies’ teeth] or [you destroy all my enemies]

Hitting an enemy on the cheek was a way of insulting people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you will insult all my enemies like someone hitting them on the jaw]

Animals attack with their teeth. Breaking their teeth takes away their power to attack. David speaks as if Yahweh would come and physically fight against the wicked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you make the wicked unable to harm me like someone breaking the teeth of a ferocious animal]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in [1:1](../001/001.md).

x.KJV: Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people. Selah.
x.YLT: Of Jehovah is this salvation; On Thy people is Thy blessing! Selah.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. The meaning of this phrase is that Yahweh is characterized by saving his people. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the savior] or [Yahweh saves his people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Please bless your people] or [You always bless your people]
